beforeChat.title: You first, then look it up
beforeChat.goal: Before looking something up, give your answer. Two minutes.
steps: When a question pops up (about work, home or plain curiosity), tap “Start” before looking it up.
Think of your answer, or say it out loud, and tap how sure you are. Nothing to write.
Look it up wherever you like (an AI, Google or asking someone) and tap whether you got it.
beforeChat.example: You wonder how often to water a cactus. You say “once a month” and tap “I think so”. You look it up: every 2–3 weeks. You tap “Sort of”.
beforeChat.done: when you tap how sure you are. It marks itself.
beforeChat.why: Trying to answer before you see the answer, even if you're wrong, makes you remember it much better later.

sayIt.title: Guess before you search
sayIt.goal: Today, before looking up a fact on your phone, bet your answer.
steps: When a question pops up (a date, a fact, how to do something), don't look it up yet.
Say your answer out loud: that's your bet.
Look it up and tap how close you were.
sayIt.example: “What year did people land on the Moon?” You bet 1972. It was 1969. Close!
sayIt.done: when you compare your bet with the real answer.
sayIt.why: Risking an answer before seeing it makes the fact stick better, even when you're wrong.

solveAlone.title: One problem, no help
solveAlone.goal: Solve a real problem yourself and use the AI only to compare at the end.
steps: Pick a problem from today you'd hand to the AI: a tricky email, an exercise, a work question.
Work on it alone for at least 15 minutes, on paper or in your head.
Tap “Start” and tap how sure you are of your solution. Then compare with the AI if you like.
solveAlone.example: “How do we share out the team's holidays without overlaps?” Your solution: a table by month, everyone picks in turns.
solveAlone.done: when you log it in the app. It marks itself.
solveAlone.why: The effort of solving something yourself is exactly what keeps the skill alive.

explain.title: Tell someone about it
explain.goal: Explain from memory something you learned this week.
steps: Pick something you learned recently: a news story, a recipe, something from work.
Tell someone about it (in person, on a call or in a voice note) without notes.
Check the source and say how much of what you said was right.
explain.example: You tell a friend about the new traffic fines. Checking later, you see you forgot the amount.
explain.done: when you've explained it and checked what you missed.
explain.why: Pulling what you learned out of memory fixes it far better than reading it again.
explain.check: How much of what you said was right?

agenda.title: Your day from memory
agenda.goal: What's on today? Say it before you open your calendar.
steps: Before opening your calendar, say out loud everything you have today and count it on your fingers.
Open the calendar and compare.
Tap how many things there were and how many you remembered.
agenda.example: You say: meeting at 10, pick up the kids, pay the power bill. The calendar had 4 things: you forgot the dentist. 3 out of 4.
agenda.done: when you compare with the calendar.
agenda.why: Every time you try to recall before looking, your memory gets practice. Looking first doesn't.
agenda.bet: How many things were on your calendar?
agenda.check: How many did you remember before looking?

shopping.title: Shop from memory
shopping.goal: Do the shopping without taking the list out of your pocket.
steps: Write your list as usual and read it through once, calmly.
Put it away and shop without taking it out.
Before paying, check the list and count how many things you remembered.
shopping.example: A list of 8 things: you remember 7, and at the till you see the coffee was missing.
shopping.done: when you've shopped without looking and checked the list at the end.
shopping.why: Trying to recall the list is real practice: each attempt makes it stick better.
shopping.bet: How many things were on the list?
shopping.check: How many did you remember without looking?

greet.title: Call them by name
greet.goal: Greet someone you met recently by their name.
steps: Think of someone you met recently: a neighbor, someone from work or church.
Before you see them, recall their name. If you saved them in the app, go over it there.
Greet them using their name.
greet.example: “Morning, Andrew! How did the move go?”
greet.done: when you've greeted someone using their name.
greet.why: Saying a name out loud is real practice. And people are glad to be remembered.

register.title: A new name
register.goal: Learn the name of someone you meet today.
steps: When you're introduced to someone, repeat their name: “Nice to meet you, Laura.”
Notice something that sets them apart and something you talked about.
Then tap “Start” and save them: the app helps you make a picture so the name sticks.
register.example: Laura, red glasses, works at a bakery. Picture: a laurel wreath in red glasses coming out of the oven.
register.done: when you save them in the app. It marks itself.
register.why: Linking a name to an exaggerated picture is a technique for remembering names that has been studied for decades.

meeting.title: Go over who's coming
meeting.goal: Before a meeting or meal, go over everyone's name.
steps: Before the get-together, go over in your head the names of who'll be there.
At the get-together, notice how many you remembered. Use at least one in conversation.
Tap how many people there were and how many names you remembered.
meeting.example: There were 5 at the parents' meeting. You remembered Caroline, George, Ms. Ines and Tom, but not Tom's dad. 4 out of 5.
meeting.done: when you count how many names you remembered.
meeting.why: Recalling names just before you need them is well-timed practice, which is when it helps most.
meeting.check: How many names did you remember?

plan.title: A trip without GPS
plan.goal: Plan with the map, put it away, and get there without it.
steps: Pick a real trip for today, ideally one you don't know well.
Tap “Start”, look at the map and write down 3 to 6 places on the way: a park, a gas station, where you turn.
Make the trip without GPS and, when you arrive, tell the app how it went.
plan.example: Home → new clinic: the church, right at the pharmacy, on to the bridge, blue building.
plan.done: when you report how it went without having followed the GPS. It marks itself.
plan.why: Finding your own way works the part of the brain that builds your mental map. Following GPS barely uses it.

return.title: Another way home
return.goal: Go home by another route, no map.
steps: On your way home today, change part of your usual route. In daylight and in an area you know.
Go by what you know: which way home is, the big streets, places you recognize.
When you arrive, say how many times you looked at the map. Zero is a perfect score.
return.example: Instead of taking the avenue, you take the street by the park and come out two blocks further on.
return.done: when you got home by another way.
return.why: Finding a new route by yourself widens your mental map; always repeating the same one doesn't.
return.check: How many times did you look at the map?

landmarks.title: Five signs on the way
landmarks.goal: Notice five things on a trip you always make and recall them in order.
steps: On a trip you make often, notice 5 things that can serve as signs: a big tree, a billboard, a mural.
When you arrive, go over them in order in your head, without looking back.
Next time you pass by, check and tap how many you had right.
landmarks.example: Corner bakery, long traffic light, yellow church, bridge, gas station. Passing again, you see the bridge came before the church: 3 out of 5.
landmarks.done: when you check on the way.
landmarks.why: People with a good sense of direction pay attention to landmarks. It's a habit you learn by practicing it.
landmarks.check: How many of the 5 did you have right?

pointHome.title: Where's home?
pointHome.goal: From a new place, point your phone toward home. The compass tells you how close you got.
steps: The first time, while at home, tap “Start” and save where it is.
When you're somewhere you don't often go, tap “Start”.
Without looking at the map, point your phone toward home and tap “Here it is”.
pointHome.example: You leave a mall, point to the left, and the compass says you were 25° off. Not bad!
pointHome.done: when you point and see your result. It marks itself.
pointHome.why: Pointing toward a place you can't see is exactly how studies measure sense of direction. Guessing and checking sharpens it.

message.title: In your own words
message.goal: Write an important message without AI and without keyboard suggestions.
steps: Pick a message from today that matters: congratulations, an apology, a reply to your boss.
Write it yourself from start to finish, without tapping the words your keyboard suggests.
Read it once, fix it and send it.
message.example: A birthday message for your aunt that isn't just “Happy birthday!”, but something only you would say.
message.done: when you've sent a message written entirely by you.
message.why: Writing is thinking: putting your ideas in order in your own words is what you lose if someone else always writes.

email.title: Your draft first
email.goal: Write a real email yourself before asking for help.
steps: Think of an email you need to send today or tomorrow.
Tap “Start” and then “New draft”. Write the whole thing (pasting is off here).
Tap “Finish draft”. If you like, compare it afterwards with what an AI would suggest.
email.example: An email asking your landlord to fix the shower: greeting, what's wrong, since when, and what you're asking for.
email.done: when you finish the draft. It marks itself.
email.why: If you write first, the AI becomes a second opinion instead of the one doing your thinking.

summary.title: Sum it up without looking
summary.goal: Write the main points of something you read or watched today, without looking back.
steps: Pick something you read or watched today: an article, a chapter, a video, a class.
Close it. Tap “Start”, then “New draft”, and write the main points in 5 to 10 lines.
Tap “Finish draft” and check the original: what did you miss?
summary.example: About sleep: “Under 7 hours hurts memory. Phone light delays sleep. Going to bed at the same time helps.”
summary.done: when you finish the draft. It marks itself.
summary.why: Summarizing from memory makes you recall and organize: two of the best-proven ways to learn.

groceries.title: The total before the till
groceries.goal: Bet your shopping total before the till tells you.
steps: While you shop, keep a running total in your head. Round it: $2.95 is $3.
Before paying, write your total here.
When the till shows the real total, enter it and see your accuracy.
groceries.example: Bread $3 + milk $4.50 + eggs $5 + coffee $9: you bet $21.50. The till says $21.20. 99 accuracy!
groceries.done: when you compare your total with the till's.
groceries.why: Doing sums with real money keeps the skill right where you need it.
groceries.bet: Your total, worked out in your head
groceries.check: The real total at the till

tip.title: Your share, no calculator
tip.goal: Work out the tip or everyone's share in your head.
steps: When a bill arrives to split, leave the calculator alone.
Do the sum in your head and write it here. Tip: 10% is moving the decimal point one place.
Check it with the calculator and enter the exact result.
tip.example: $84 split 4 ways: $80 ÷ 4 = $20 and $4 ÷ 4 = $1. You bet $21. Spot on!
tip.done: when you check your sum with the calculator.
tip.why: Breaking a sum into easy pieces is a skill that fades if the calculator always does it.
tip.bet: Your sum, done in your head

budget.title: How much did I spend this week?
budget.goal: Work out your spending this week and compare it with your bank.
steps: Without checking your bank, go over the week day by day: what you bought and roughly what it cost.
Add it up and write your total here.
Open your bank app or receipts and enter the real total.
budget.example: Groceries $120, gas $60, lunches $45… You bet $260. The bank says $290.
budget.done: when you compare your total with the real figure.
budget.why: Working it out before looking gives you a feel for amounts, and you learn where your money goes.

arrival.title: What time will I get there?
arrival.goal: Before you leave, bet your arrival time.
steps: Before leaving, work out in your head how long it takes and write here when you'll arrive.
Make the trip.
When you arrive, tap “Check”: the current time is already filled in.
arrival.example: It's 3:50. 25 minutes of travel plus 10 waiting for the bus: you bet 4:25. You arrive at 4:28. 85 accuracy!
arrival.done: when you compare your time with when you arrived.
arrival.why: Adding hours and minutes in your head is an everyday sum the phone habit takes away.

estimate.title: How much do you think it is?
estimate.goal: Guess a price or a figure before looking it up.
steps: Today, before looking up a price or any number, stop.
Write your guess here, as specific as you can.
Look up the real figure and enter it to see your accuracy.
estimate.example: “How much is a mid-size fridge?” You bet $600. The store says $750: 80 accuracy.
estimate.done: when you compare your guess with the real figure.
estimate.why: Guessing and checking sharpens your feel for amounts: every miss brings you closer next time.

phone.title: A number by heart
phone.goal: Learn the phone number of someone close and dial it without your contacts.
steps: Pick someone important whose number you don't know: your partner, a child, your mom.
Learn it in chunks of 3 or 4 digits, repeating it out loud.
Hours later, dial it without opening your contacts.
phone.example: 555 · 201 · 1234: you repeat it three times in the morning and dial it from memory in the afternoon.
phone.done: when you've dialed it without looking at your contacts.
phone.why: Recalling it hours later is what makes it stick. And it helps the day you don't have your phone.

askWay.title: Ask the way
askWay.goal: Get somewhere by asking a person instead of using the map.
steps: Next time you don't know how to get somewhere nearby, put your phone away.
Ask someone: a shopkeeper, a security guard, a neighbor. Repeat the directions out loud.
When you arrive, say how many times you took out your phone. Zero is perfect.
askWay.example: “Two blocks straight, left at the pharmacy, white building.” You: “Two straight, pharmacy, left, white.”
askWay.done: when you've arrived following someone's directions.
askWay.why: Following spoken directions makes you build the map in your head, exactly what GPS does for you.
askWay.check: How many times did you take out your phone?

teach.title: Teach someone
teach.goal: Teach something you know how to do, without looking anything up.
steps: Think of something you do well: a recipe, a phone trick, changing a tire.
Explain it step by step to someone, with no videos or instructions.
Ask them to do it or repeat it back, and say how well it went.
teach.example: You teach your nephew to make pancakes: flour, eggs, milk, mix, pour, flip.
teach.done: when the other person has had a go.
teach.why: Explaining from memory makes you recall and organize; that's why they say teaching is learning twice.
teach.check: How well did the other person do?

birthday.title: Three birthdays
birthday.goal: Recall three birthdays without checking the calendar.
steps: Think of three people close to you.
Say or write each one's birthday.
Check them on the calendar and count how many you got right.
birthday.example: Mom: March 12. Charles: August 5. Lucy: November 30? The calendar says November 3. 2 out of 3.
birthday.done: when you've checked the three dates.
birthday.why: Trying to recall and then correcting is the most effective way to make a fact stay.
birthday.check: How many did you get right?

handwrite.title: A handwritten note
handwrite.goal: Handwrite a short note for someone.
steps: Grab paper and a pencil or pen.
Write a note of thanks, encouragement or affection. At least three sentences.
Hand it over or leave it where they'll find it.
handwrite.example: “Thanks for taking me to the doctor on Tuesday. I don't say it much, but you made my day. I owe you a coffee.”
handwrite.done: when the note has reached its person.
handwrite.why: Writing by hand, with no spell-check or suggestions, makes you think through each sentence first.

clock.title: How long to go?
clock.goal: Work out in your head how many minutes until your next meal. The app checks it instantly.
steps: Look at the time just once.
Work out in your head how many minutes until your next meal.
Enter the meal time and your minutes here: the app tells you if you got it.
clock.example: It's 10:35 and lunch is at 1:00. To 11 is 25 minutes, plus 2 hours: 145 minutes.
clock.done: when the app checks your sum.
clock.why: Counting in hours and minutes is an everyday sum we nearly always leave to the phone.
clock.bet: What time is your next meal?
clock.check: How many minutes to go? (in your head)

about.title: About Handfly
about.origin: The name comes from aviation. Pilots who almost always fly on autopilot slowly lose the ability to fly by hand. That's why they practice hand-flying, even when they don't need to.
about.idea: The same happens to us with AI, GPS and calculators. They are great tools, but if we never do things without them, we stop knowing how. Handfly helps you practice on purpose, with tasks from your real life, so those skills are still there when you need them.
can: Help you build the habit of trying first before asking an AI.
Help you remember what you learn and the names of people you meet, using well-studied techniques.
Give you real practice finding your way, writing and doing math in everyday situations.
Show you, with honest data, how much you solve on your own and how much you hand off.
cannot: It won't make you smarter. No exercise has shown that, so be wary of anyone who promises it.
It doesn't improve memory "in general": it improves what you practice and very similar things.
It doesn't replace real-life practice. What counts is what you do outside the app.
It isn't a treatment. If you're worried about your memory or attention, talk to a health professional.
about.privacy: Everything you write (questions, names, notes, routes, texts) is stored only on this device. There are no accounts, no servers receiving your data, no ads and no usage analytics. You decide whether to download a backup and where to keep it.
about.ethics: There is no endless content. A session lasts 5 to 10 minutes and, when it ends, the app says goodbye and invites you to go practice. There's one optional reminder a day and no guilt-tripping messages. Your streak gets one rest day a week.
about.open: Handfly is free and open source under the MIT license. Every new module must explain why its practice helps in real life and cite the evidence behind it.

celebrate.topRank: You've reached the top rank. Now it's your turn to teach.

welcome.title: Switch off the autopilot
welcome.p1: Pilots fly by hand now and then so they don't lose the skill. Handfly does the same for what you now hand over to AI, GPS and calculators.
welcome.p2: No memory games: every mission is something real from your day. And yes, you'll score points.
welcome.pickLead: Pick what matters most to you. Your missions will mostly come from there.
welcome.pickNote: You can change this anytime in Settings.
welcome.how1b: Something specific from your life, with steps and an example. A few minutes.
welcome.how2b: Before doing it you place your bet: the shopping total, your arrival time. Afterwards you see your accuracy from 0 to 100 and chase your record.
welcome.how3b: Every mission adds real flight minutes. From student pilot to instructor, with your wings.
welcome.privacy: Everything stays on your phone: no accounts, no ads, no tracking.
